title: The DOM
summary: The DOM is the browser's model of the page parts. JavaScript can find and change those parts.
introduction: The DOM is the browser's model of the page parts. JavaScript can find and change those parts. Think of the page as a tree with branches. Find one heading, change its text, then add a new item to a list.
learningObjectives: Describe the DOM as a tree that JavaScript modifies through the document object
Select elements with querySelector, querySelectorAll and getElementById
Change text, attributes, classes and inline styles safely
Create, insert and remove elements and run scripts after the page has loaded

blocks.text:
The browser turns markup such as `
  • Milk
` into objects: a `ul` element object with a `li` child, which in turn holds a text node. The whole tree hangs from `document`, a global object every script can use. Each element object has properties that reflect its content and attributes, and changing a property changes the page. Knowing [HTML elements](/tutorials/html/elements) and [attributes](/tutorials/html/attributes) matters here, because the DOM mirrors them one for one.

`document.querySelector(selector)` returns the first element matching a CSS selector, or `null` when there is none; `document.querySelectorAll(selector)` returns a `NodeList` of every match. `getElementById("id")` is a fast alternative for ids (note: no `#`). Because the examples below run in a sandbox with an empty page, each one first builds the elements it works with; in a real page they already exist.

`textContent` reads or replaces the text inside an element; whatever you assign is shown literally. `innerHTML` reads or replaces the markup, so the browser parses tags in the string and creates elements. Use `textContent` for anything that comes from a user or a server: assigning such text to `innerHTML` lets an attacker inject markup and scripts into your page (a **cross-site scripting** attack).

`setAttribute` and `getAttribute` work with any attribute; common ones such as `href`, `id` and `value` are also plain properties. `classList` adds, removes and toggles classes without string juggling, and is the preferred way to change appearance: put the CSS in a class and switch the class. `dataset` exposes `data-*` attributes as properties. The `style` property sets inline styles for the rare values computed at runtime, such as a progress bar width.

`document.createElement(tag)` makes a detached element; fill it in, then insert it with `append` (end of the parent), `prepend` (start), `before` or `after` (next to a sibling). `remove()` takes an element out of the tree. Building elements from data in a loop is the pattern behind every dynamic list, table and gallery.
Try it on a real page

The page below has real markup to work on. The script changes the heading, adds a highlighted item to the list and colours the note. Edit it and press Run: try removing the first item, or adding a class to every `li` with a loop over `querySelectorAll`.

blocks.text: The browser runs a script the moment it reaches the `<script>` tag. A script in `<head>` therefore runs before `<body>` has been parsed, and `querySelector` finds nothing. There are three fixes: put the script at the end of `<body>`, load an external file with `defer`, or wait for the `DOMContentLoaded` event. The example shows the problem and the event-based fix in one page.

blocks.title: Cannot read properties of null
blocks.text: `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'textContent')` almost always means a selector found nothing: either the script ran before the element existed, or the selector is wrong (a typo in the id, or `getElementById("#title")` with a `#` that only `querySelector` understands). Log the result of the selector first; if it is `null`, fix the timing or the selector.

questions.question: Which call returns a single element, or null if nothing matches?
questions.explanation: querySelector returns the first match or null. querySelectorAll always returns a NodeList, even an empty one.

questions.question: Assigning text typed by a user to `element.innerHTML` is safe because browsers block scripts in it.
questions.explanation: innerHTML parses markup, and attacker-controlled markup can inject elements and run code (cross-site scripting). Use textContent for user-provided text.
